label: Moral and epistemic parity: distinguish categorical force from irreducible favoring
summary: Read the primary-author arguments of Richard Rowland (2013, JESP), Jonas Olson (2018, Stockholm University accepted chapter) and Alex Murphy (2020, UCL open-access paper). Rowland defends a categorical-epistemic-reason route from a strong moral error theory denying all categorical reasons. Olson supplies a concrete functional alternative: reasons for belief are performance-to-belief-function standards, not irreducibly normative favoring, so moral-reason denial can coexist with some epistemic reasons. Murphy challenges this disparity by applying the error theorist's own rhetorical-authority argument to epistemic discourse and by testing whether moral judgments can also be understood functionally. Existing F6 is only a thin reason existential, and the stronger preference-independent epistemic authority still differs from irreducibility; neither can be silently identified with an irreducibly categorical reason. The current two-kind adoption model shows moral reason denial and epistemic adoption reasons coexisting, but has no functional/irreducibility distinction. Two research forks now identified: global irreducible-reason denial plus irreducible epistemic witness is inconsistent; moral-only error theory remains compatible with an epistemic witness unless a distinct positive moral reason or relevant cross-domain transfer is supplied. The belief-inquiry-action feedback loop illustrates practical interaction but does not by itself add a moral norm. No new attributed claim, theorem, worldview defeat or root premise closure. Detailed comparison in docs/notes/self-undermining-views.md.
blocker: Register sense-distinct irreducible, preference-independent and function-relative epistemic reasons with nonvacuous controls; link a specifically scoped error-theory package to its actual normative denial and test Olson's asymmetric functional explanation against Murphy's authority-parity argument. A separate substantive step is needed from any epistemic witness to an actual moral reason, beyond the shared reason genus.
